en: Obeisance to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
In the *Śrī Pūvallī Pañcavaṇigī*, composed by the venerable Siddhananjeśa Śivācārya, [which is] the play of the dialogue between Consciousness and Density (*Cidghanasaṃvādavilasita*).
In the *Śrī Śivasiddhāntacandrikā*, [the section on the Introduction].
[Invocation] Homage to Śiva, who is accompanied by Umā, and who transcends the six paths.
Salutation to the Brahman of the six stations, who possesses the thirty-six principles as his *liṅga*. || 1 ||
The support of the universe, whose form is the universe, and who has the nature of the material cause of the universe.
I always salute Viśveśvarī, the bestower of all knowledge. || 2 ||
The one who inaugurated the tradition of the Great Sutra of Five Colors.
I pay homage with devotion to the supreme Guru, the perfected Caitanya of Pūrvallī. || 3 ||
That Lord Śiva, the master of Kailāsa and the illustrious Nīlakaṇṭha, having descended to earth in ancient times at the request of Vyāsa, established the Śaiva Āgamas.
By churning the ocean of that Sūtra and producing the purifying nectar of the Bhāṣya, he nourished the entire world by bestowing it; to that gentle Guru of the Earth (Bhūguru), I pay homage.
May the venerable Śrī Bhagavatpāda, the illustrious Nīlakaṇṭha, the preceptor of the world, be victorious!
He who established the doctrine of the non-duality of Śiva upon the earth.
He who was born from the lotus-hand of the venerable Sadguru Nīlakaṇṭha Yati,
whom they know as the Lord of the noble lion-throne of the Bṛhanmaṭha in Pūrvalli;
We perpetually offer salutations to that Guru named Cidghana, by whom the great bamboo-pole of the Cola kingdom, which was his own support, was uprooted.
I perpetually bow to the venerable Guru, known as Aghora Śivācārya, who blazes with fierce asceticism, for the sake of attaining glorious prosperity, victory, and spiritual perfection.
This is the dialogue between the King of Chola and the Embodiment of Consciousness, consisting of answers to the questions of Emperor Satyendra Chola,
which brings benefit to the worlds.
Having compiled [the teachings] in the form of a treatise, Śivācārya, the foremost among the wise and a master of the Siddhas, composes this *Śivasiddhāntacandrikā*.
May the *Śivasiddhāntacandrikā*, which produces the nectar of Śiva-bliss and illuminates the knowledge of Śiva, bestow prosperity, auspiciousness, and well-being.
In former times, O Great King, there was a sovereign ruler of the Colamaṇḍala, a most excellent emperor named Śrīmat Satyendra. || 11 ||
This very King Satyendra is like the Lord of the Gods;
his queen, named Amṛtavatī, is like Śacī herself.
The city named Dharmavatī was like the celestial Amarāvatī manifest on earth;
its king was the crest-jewel of monarchs, Jayanta, who was ever victorious. (13)
His guru was the teacher Cidghana, who was like Bṛhaspati in brilliance in person;
he was a knower of the truth of the Vedas and Vedānta, and an expert in all the scriptures. || 14 ||
He was renowned as a teacher of the great science of Śiva’s non-duality, an instructor of the Dharma, and a forest fire to the vast jungle of opposing disputants. || 15 ||
He who was adorned by his status as a disciple of the illustrious Nīlakaṇṭha-paṭṭa.
Having attained the lordship of the Pūlī-siṃhāsana upon the surface of the earth, [he shall rule]. || 16 ||
Having established the doctrine of the non-duality of Śiva as proclaimed by the Vedas, and having taught it for the benefit of those seeking liberation, he shines resplendent. (17)
By the mere grace of him, the prosperities of the kingdom became equal to the prosperities of heaven, serving as the abode of all happiness. (18)
The crops were free from blight and affliction, and the people were without calamity;
the sacred fields of the gods were endowed with worship and recitation as prescribed in the Vedas. (19)
All the ritual activities of the hermitage were performed without hindrance by those devoted to austerity;
and the royal lineage of Satyendra was filled with a portion of merit.

Thus endowed with such companions, the illustrious and supreme king Satyendra once approached the most excellent of true gurus, the embodiment of consciousness (cidghana), who was possessed of great majesty.

It was made resplendent by all the heraldic titles, including the swaying of banners, white umbrellas, yak-tail fans, and arches, as well as the Nandi-bull, the victory banner, and other such emblems.
Accompanied by his retinue, he returned to the capital with great festivity and true devotion, and performed the worship according to the prescribed ritual.
Highly gratified by that worship was Śrī Citghanaśivācārya, the destroyer of the distress of the virtuous, who is ever intent upon protecting his devotees.
Having observed the descent of power (śaktipāta) upon that great king, Satyendra, he joyfully initiated him along with his family.

For the sake of attaining the eightfold coverings (aṣṭāvaraṇa) and for the increase of the fivefold conduct (pañcācāra), preceded by the wearing of the liṅga as proclaimed in the Vīraśaiva tradition; || 26 ||
Having caused him to understand the great and most exalted Great Mantra (Mahāmantra) known as the Five-Syllabled Name of Śiva,
the preceptor of the earth showed him the path to liberation.
Then, by the power of his initiation and endowed with the splendor of the great mantra, this very King Satyendra attained perfection in the knowledge of Śiva. 28.

Joyfully prostrating like a staff before the most excellent Guru, the embodiment of auspicious consciousness, he, being well-disciplined and with palms joined in reverence, questioned him with great devotion. (29)
[Thus ends the introductory chapter in the Śivasiddhāntacandrikā composed by the venerable Jagadguru Siddhananjeśa Śivācārya, the sovereign of the illustrious Pūvallī Bhāṣya-siṃhāsana.]
[The First Chapter]
He said: O illustrious Guru, O Great Lord, intent upon protecting your disciples, knower of the reality of the Śiva-siddhānta, destroyer of the doubts of your disciples! (1)
They say that this entire world, including all that moves and is stationary, is without a Lord;
having severed my doubt regarding this, O Lord, speak the certain truth to me.
Cidghana said:
"O illustrious one, O best of universal monarchs, you have asked well.
For the benefit of all the worlds, I shall now definitively explain that which you have requested."
There exists a certain Creator of the world, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss;
self-luminous and independent, consisting of both the sentient and the insentient.
This entire universe, including all things mobile and immobile, is preceded by an intelligent creator,
because it is an effect and because it is an object of cognition, just like a jar and other such objects in the world.
The state of being an effect is established from its configuration and from its possession of activity;
likewise, the state of being an object of knowledge is established from its being an object of cognition. (6)
The causality of the world is not accepted for the Pradhāna because it is insentient;
furthermore, there is grammatical coreferentiality between agency and sentience. (7)
In the absence of that [consciousness], how can the Primordial Matter (pradhāna) be asserted to possess agency? For, being dependent upon consciousness, it lacks independence. (8)
Time, too, is not accepted as an agent because it is likewise [insentient];
nor is agency admitted for action, since it is itself dependent.

Independence consists in not being employed by another, while the state of being an employer of instruments and so forth constitutes the independence of the agent; for this independence does not depend upon instruments and the like.
And since that [apūrva] is established through the granting of its fruit, this other agent—Śiva—is proven to be independent and conscious. (11)
Because he is independent in all his actions and because of the fear of infinite regress, another agent for Maheśvara is not established in reality. (12)
Śiva alone is the creator of the universe; no creator of him is found.
Śiva alone is the sustainer of the universe; no sustainer of him is found. || 13 ||
Śiva alone is the destroyer of the universe; there is no destroyer of him.
Śiva alone is the Lord of the universe; there is no lord of him. (14)
He said:
"O Teacher of the World, all this that has been spoken by you is known to me; however, O Lord, please dispel this doubt of mine with authoritative proof. (15)
O Compassionate One, tell me in brief: what is the material cause, the efficient cause, and the instrumental cause in the production of the universe? Please explain all of this.
Cidghana said:
"O illustrious Satyendra, you have raised a worthy doubt; I shall provide its resolution—listen with an attentive mind. (17)
Qualified by that power which consists of both the conscious and the unconscious, Śiva—the Self of all—becomes the cause as both the material and the efficient cause. (18)
The material cause (upādāna) is the supreme power, and this world is that which is to be produced (upādeya);
its agent and efficient cause (nimitta) is declared to be Paramaśiva. || 19 ||
Just as a spider proceeds to a twofold causality with respect to its web,
so too does this Supreme Śiva, distinguished by His power, proceed in that same manner.
Without Śakti, He is not able to perform any action in the world;
endowed with identity with her, Sāmba is called the creator of all. (21)
The effect is predominant because of its power, and the cause is predominant because of its own nature;
yet, through the union of Śiva and Śakti, that [effect] is neither an agent nor an instrument.
Because power loses its autonomy, agency is not established at all;
rather, causality is properly understood as consisting in the nature of the material cause (upādāna).
The power (śakti) and the rest, ending with earth, are supported by the Supreme Reality (paratattva).
Why? Because [otherwise] they would be without support; for in the world, objects such as jars are seen to have a support. (24)
The power under discussion is dependent on something, because it is a property;
just as potness is seen to be dependent on a pot, so too is this power. (25)
Its nature as *dharmatva* (the state of being a property) is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it possesses activity;
for Śiva is the agent of the universe precisely because he is the material cause of the universe. (26)
Just as in the world, that which is observed, such as a jar and so forth, is characterized by its distinction [from others].
Or rather, is the Supreme Śiva indeed endowed with appropriation because of his status as an agent? (27)
Just as a potter, who is superior to clay, is seen to produce jars and other such objects, so too [the Lord], through general pervasion, is endowed with the material cause of the universe. (28)

Śiva himself attains perfection; therefore, for the sake of establishing that [attainment], he is the material cause, because primary action, time, and so forth are not so [capable] according to reason. (29)
Upādāna is indeed the eternal power residing in Brahman;
she is the auxiliary for Śiva to create the world as the material cause. (30)
Having the nature of non-difference from Śiva and the nature of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa),
she is established by those who have reached the further shore of the scriptures as being innate and of the nature of dharma.
Co(? said:
"All this is well-established by the means of valid cognition known as inference;
therefore, O Teacher of the World, explain to me the authority of the Veda. (32)
Cidghana said:
That which is a non-human utterance is called the Veda;
therefore, it is inherently authoritative because it is the instruction of the Supreme Trustworthy One.
All the Vedas proclaim the very existence of the Lord;
therein, the collection of Upaniṣads, beginning with the Īśāvāsya, remains ever awake.
Śaṅkara is the trustworthy authority for the Veda, which is established as valid by itself; he is of great intelligence, his own means of knowledge, self-luminous, and self-proven. (35)
The Vedas and likewise the Āgamas were clearly articulated in the past by Śiva himself in the form of his own breath; therefore, they are self-validating authorities. (36)
By stating that [the word], its existence would be established as something to be abandoned;
therefore, its meaning is established through indicators such as the opening statement (upakrama) and so forth. (37)
This very point is distinguished in the Śivādvaita-siddhānta;
for within that system, which consists of both duality and non-duality, all the Vedas find their harmonious reconciliation. (38)
Therefore, according to the method taught in the non-duality of Śiva, that existence of Śiva—which is established by all means of valid cognition—is thoroughly proven by all Vedic statements. (39)
Impelled by the statement "May I be many, may I procreate," that which is of the nature of the locus of egoity is called the agent, while the other is called the object. (40)
Due to the predominance of the "I" (ahaṃtā) aspect, he is designated as Śiva;
due to the predominance of the "this" (idaṃtā) aspect, he is called Śakti by the wise. (41)
Due to the identity of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) and "this-ness" (idaṃtā), there is non-difference between Śiva and Śakti;
and the unity of power and the possessor of power is like that of the moon and its moonlight.
That by whose light the universe shines and in which alone it finds delight—
that indeed is the Supreme Brahman, endowed with Śiva and Śakti.
By such statements as "His power is supreme," which are pregnant with their essential meaning, this Supreme Brahman known as Śiva is declared through its own authoritative means. (44)
Co asked:
"How is Śiva—who is designated as the Supreme Brahman and distinguished by all powers—said to be known by the name Liṅgasthala? Please tell me that. (45)
Cidghana said:
Because of its vastness and because of its capacity to nourish, it is sung of as "Brahma-sthala.
That wherein one stands firm and dissolves is called the place known as Brahma. (46)
That very same thing has been stated in the Āgamas and established in the Vedas;
it is also cited in the Sūtra: "And because of the designation of [His] abodes and so forth. (2.3.1) [47]

That which was declared in the Brahma-sūtra, "from which [proceeds] the birth and so forth of this [world]," namely the mark consisting of the world's birth and so forth, is here designated by the word "liṅga. (48)
That wherein this entire universe, both moving and unmoving, dissolves and goes, that alone is the *liṅga*, that is Brahman, and that is called the principle of Śiva (Śivatattva). || 49 ||
Therefore, the *liṅga*, which is the supreme Brahman, should be investigated through the understanding of the Vedas;
it should indeed be worn upon the body according to the prescribed rules and worshipped as accomplished through the gradual stages.

It should be heard from the words of the Vedas, reflected upon through logical reasoning, and meditated upon through continuous contemplation in accordance with the subtle signs of the vital breath (prāṇaliṅga). || 51 ||
One should cultivate the symbol of existence through the experience of the state of "I am He";
one should perceive with one's own self the supreme abode as distinguished by its power.
The knot of the heart is pierced, all doubts are severed,
and one's karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen.
Thus, in [the work] composed by the venerable Jagadguru Siddhananjesa Sivacharya, the sovereign of the lion-throne of the Pūvallī lineage and the founder of the tradition of the *Śrīpañcavarṇasūtra*.
In the *Śivasiddhāntacandrikā*, which shines with the dialogue between Cit and Ghana,
this is the first chapter.
[Now begins the second chapter.
Co said: "O Teacher of the World, that power which has been described as having the form of the material cause of the universe—"
O Lord, I have a great curiosity to hear its true nature.
O Great Lord, please explain with authoritative evidence, based on the understanding of cause and effect, how all my doubts may be completely resolved. (2)
Cidghana said:
"Well asked, O illustrious one, O sovereign, best of kings!
I shall explain to you all that which is the essence of the Vedas and the Āgamas."

The eternal power of Brahman, having assumed the nature of both consciousness and unconsciousness, is indeed declared to be the material cause of the universe consisting of the conscious and the unconscious. (4)
Through the expansion of power (śakti), the creation of the universe occurs;
likewise, through its contraction, the dissolution of the universe occurs. || 5 ||
Stability occurs through a state of equilibrium between expansion and contraction;
the sequence of this process is described by the analogy of the limbs of a tortoise. (6)
Having undergone transformation through the mere proximity of Śiva,
Śakti assumes the form of the effect and manifests in the form of the universe.
That by whose light the universe shines, and in whom alone it finds delight—
She is proclaimed by such Vedic texts as "Supreme is His power" (parāsya śaktiḥ).
The abandonment of one's own nature and the establishment in another nature—
that is declared as "effect" by the wise proponents of the theory of the pre-existent effect (satkāryavāda).
Just as in the world an effect is seen to arise from the abandonment of the nature of clay and the assumption of an internal form such as a jar, so too is this [universal] effect intended.
That which, by serving as the substratum for the state of the effect, brings about the production of the effect, is designated as the "cause" and specifically termed the "material cause. (11)
Just as gold is the cause by virtue of being the substratum for the state of a snake or an earring, so too is Śakti held to be the material cause of the universe.
That which produces an effect by serving as the substratum for the grasping [of the aggregates] is the cause known as the "efficient" (nimitta); specifically, that is the agent (kartṛ). || 13 ||
And among all causes, he who is independent and conscious is alone the agent of an effect, such as a jar, just like a potter. (14)
The Supreme Śiva is declared to be both the material cause and the efficient cause of the universe due to his association with Śakti, just as a spider is known to be the source of its web. (15)
In the aspect of Śakti, it is the material cause (upādāna), and in the aspect of Śiva, it is the efficient cause (nimitta);
because of the unity of both, the cause is said to be of a dual nature.
This effect is gross power, while the cause is subtle power;
because of its grossness it is the "to-be-adopted" (upādeya), whereas the material cause (upādāna) is due to its subtlety.
This individual soul (jīva) has the effect as its limiting adjunct (upādhi), while the Lord (īśvara) has the cause as his limiting adjunct;
due to this disparity between cause and effect, there is a difference between Śiva and the jīva.

In this established doctrine, it is not asserted that this world, which is the effect, is either non-different from its cause, nor is it said to be absolutely different from the cause designated as Śiva. (19)
That being so, the effect would be either existent, non-existent, or both existent and non-existent.
If it is an existent effect, is it so by virtue of the cause's existence or by virtue of the effect's own existence? (20)
If that [effect] were to exist [simultaneously] with the cause, how could there be a difference in their existence?
That which is designated as the effect would then be distinct from the existence of the cause. (21)
If it is argued that the effect is thus designated as such, then it would be non-existent; for it is logical that an effect devoid of existence is indeed non-existent. (22)
If the effect were already existent [prior to its production], then the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda) would be rendered futile.
Furthermore, if that existence of the effect were distinct from the existence of the cause, [the two could not be related]. (23)
Or else, it [the universal] must exist either in the form of being or in the form of non-being.
If it exists in the form of being, how can there be a single universal while there is a distinction [between individuals]? (24)
If it were distinct by way of having a non-existent form, it would not be called "existence.
If the effect were held to be non-existent [prior to its production], then that would not be an effect at all. (25)
The son of a barren woman is not intended to be an effect for anyone in reality;
likewise, antecedent non-existence cannot be an effect, because its production is impossible. (26)
Just as there is no connection whatsoever between the son of a barren woman and his causal factors,
so too, because it is as indefinable as a void, there is no act of production.

If it is argued that a distinction exists even though the effect is non-existent, then what is this distinction? If it is said to be its connection with the causal factors (*kāraka*), that is not so. (28)
Whatever specific relation it has is said to be its [relation];
if its possession of the act of being born is the specific [relation], then it is so. (29)
But for that [cause] which has reached the state of having the aforementioned defects, there is no prevention;
even if its distinction were the possession of a connection with existence, that is not effective. (30)
Even then, the previously mentioned fault applies to this without a doubt.
Therefore, that which is non-existent cannot be an effect, and the state of being both existent and non-existent is not tenable.
The aforementioned arrival of the two defects would then occur;
therefore, having cast aside envy regarding both the effect and the cause at that time, [one should proceed]. (32)
Thus, non-difference should be understood precisely because difference is impossible;
therefore, there is no absolute distinctness, for it is accepted that there is both difference and non-difference. (33)
The collection of effects does not differ from its cause in reality;
likewise, the distinction between cause and effect as well as the exclusion of other causal factors [is unreal]. (34)
Arising and destruction, as well as causal efficiency and the distinction between name and form—all this is solely by means of speech alone. (35)
Therefore, all this modification, joined with name, form, and so forth, is merely a verbal handle; it is indeed only the form of the cause.

In this doctrine of the non-duality of Śiva, the effect is indeed the cause itself, since it possesses a nature non-different from its cause; so it is proclaimed by the most excellent of scholars. (37)
Therefore, because it makes known all consciousness through the consciousness of the cause, the statement of the proposition is logical; there is no doubt whatsoever. (38)
Thus, that cause is one; it is neither diverse nor of a dual nature.
Diversity is not tenable in any way, because the substratum and so forth cannot be established. (39)
For if difference were already known, there would result the knowledge of the distinction between the substratum and so forth;
and if the substratum and so forth were already known through their distinctness, there would be the cognition of difference. (40)
For difference and non-difference are indeed accepted in the form of cause and effect;
therefore, the cause is eternal, one, and without a second.

Even though a distinction is observed on the ground between clay and the like and the potter and the like, the potter and others are required [as causes] because that [clay, etc. lacks consciousness. (42)
Likewise, in this case, no other cause consisting of consciousness is required for the Supreme Self, who is characterized by the powers of consciousness and matter. (43)
Even though He is conscious, Śiva himself, like a potter,
does not require another unconscious cause equal to clay as a material cause.
Therefore, from that inconceivable power, due to its nature as both conscious and unconscious, the entire universe— comprising both the conscious and the unconscious— is produced as its effect.
And the reality of that which has the nature of consciousness is established by all means of valid cognition;
it is declared in the Śruti: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone. (46)
A cause is declared to be of an existent nature, and not of a non-existent nature in reality;
for the son of a barren woman is not called the cause of anything by the wise. (47)
If it is argued that the non-existent becomes the cause of all things through its own power, [we reply:
that power does not belong to the non-existent, for we observe that only a seed which is existent [can produce a sprout]. (48)

Just as the sprout of a seed that is existent in nature is held to arise through its power, so too the arising of the phenomenal world (prapañca) from the existent Brahman is held to occur through its power. || 49 ||
If it is argued that the universe arises as an unreal effect through the power of *śakti*, then is that *śakti* existent, non-existent, or both? (50)
If that power were existent, how could it have the son of a barren woman as its locus?
For a locus is observed for what exists, but it is never seen for what does not exist in this world.
If it were non-existent, how could power bring about the accomplishment of an effect? And how could the son of a barren woman be the accomplisher of an effect in that case? (52)
How could the production of ripe fruit occur from a sky-flower that is non-existent?
For properties such as being capable of being carried out belong to that which has the nature of existence, not to that which is non-existent. (53)
If it were thus both existent and non-existent, there would be the occurrence of two faults;
therefore, by its own power, that [entity] is neither effect nor cause. (54)
The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being;
therefore, the doctrine of non-existence is improper, being mere idle chatter and lacking any logical foundation.
By such statements as "it does not exist" and so forth, the subtle state of the effect is taught, like seeds of grass and other plants absorbed into the earth during the summer season. (56)
The subtle state of the effect, when merged within the cause, is designated as "non-existent" (asat);
therefore, by all the statements of the Śruti, its nature as Being (sat-rūpatva) is firmly established. || 57 ||
Everything endowed with true perception is awakened by the existence of Brahman;
it is established in the non-duality of Śiva as the very nature of the power of existence. || 58 ||
Thus, because it is the Supreme Brahman endowed with consciousness and is the locus of supreme love, it is called "the mass of bliss" (ānandaghana);
and because it bestows liberation upon the individual soul (jīva), it is so described. || 59 ||

If there were no Brahman consisting of bliss, and if Brahman were not of the nature of existence and consciousness, then how could the distinction between bondage and liberation be logically established? (60)

Since the continuum of the individual soul (jīvātman) is bound by the ripening of past actions (karma), and because [the Lord] would not be the object of supreme love [for that soul], how could He be the bestower of liberation? (51)

Therefore, Sāmba, whose defining characteristic is existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda), is celebrated through attributes consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss, which are characterized as being, appearing, and being dear to the self. || 62 ||
By means of the statement "May I become many," he, through the power of his own energy,
created this entire universe consisting of the thirty-six principles (tattvas).
Śakti, Sadāśiva, Īśa, Vidyā, Māyā, and the others are the causes;
likewise, Vidyā, Rāga, Kāla, Niyati, and Kalā. (64)
The Puruṣa, Pradhāna, the intellect (buddhi), the ego (ahaṃtva), the mind (mānasa), the five organs of perception, and the five organs of action; || 65 ||

The five subtle elements (tanmātras), the [five] sense organs, the mind, the intellect, ego, and the five gross elements—thus was this collection of thirty-six principles directly created from Śiva. (66)
Having created that, he entered into it himself with his inner self;
having entered, he exists in universal form, endowed with name, form, and action.
Through the supreme power that is the support of all, Śiva shines as consisting of the universe;
through his own devotion, he [realizes] that power of the divine Self which is concealed by its own qualities. 68.
They perceive [the truth] through the yoga of meditation by means of the experience of the identity between the sign (liṅga) and the body (aṅga).
Therefore, with every effort, be devoted to the yoga of meditation. 69.
[Thus ends the second chapter of the Śivasiddhāntacandrikā, composed by the illustrious Jagadguru Siddhananjeśa Śivācārya, the sovereign of the throne of the Pūvallī Bhāṣya.]
He said: O Śrīguru, ocean of compassion, friend of the distressed, great Lord!
How do the yogins of meditation perceive the power whose essence is Brahman? (1)
Therefore, O Great Lord, let that which is well-accorded by the Vedas and Agamas be told—
that for the sake of which those seeking liberation always strive with devotion and self-restraint.
Cidghana said:
O illustrious Satyendra, these words you have asked concern that which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those seeking release, both in this world and the next.
I shall declare all of that to you— the definitive meaning of all scriptures,
the most secret of secrets in the world, the non-duality of Śiva, the auspicious state.
Yogas have been described as manifold, distinguished by divisions such as action (karma) and knowledge (jñāna);
among all of them, the yoga of meditation (dhyānayoga) prescribed in the scriptures is preeminent. || 5 ||
For meditation is the direct means for perceiving the power of the divine self;
the Śiva-power, which is unfailing, conforms to that meditation.
Devotion to Śiva arises through merits accumulated over ten million births;
from devotion, knowledge is born, and from knowledge comes liberation—of this there is no doubt. (7)
Some rely upon karma, while others rely upon knowledge;
we, however, by virtue of the perfection of devotion, rely upon the yoga of meditation.
In the yoga of meditation accessible through devotion, there is a synthesis of action and knowledge;
therefore, in this path declared by the scriptures, all the Vedas find their harmonious convergence.
Sāṃkhya-yoga that is devoid of a Lord would fall into the path of ridicule;
for in the absence of a Lord, the purpose of yoga cannot in any way be logically established.
For dualists such as the Naiyāyikas and others, the meaning of "yoga" as [the state of] being joined is not tenable;
however, when the oneness of Brahman is understood through the meaning of the word "yoga," there exists the knowledge of duality [as a contrast]. (11)
How could that [meditation] be a means to accomplishment, given the contradiction between duality and unity?
For the purpose of ceasing the perception of duality, meditation upon that [unity] is prescribed. (12)
Through external worship, internal worship becomes directly firm;
and by that [internal worship], the oneness of Śiva and the individual soul, which is termed "direct realization," is attained. (13)
Therefore, a devotee engaged in worship shall become liberated;
one who desires liberation should, with true devotion, take recourse to the yoga of meditation. (14)
Some, having fully resorted to renunciation through the path of non-duality, are satisfied with mere reflection and proclaim the knowledge of liberation. || 15 ||
For those who are satisfied with that [limited] knowledge and who possess the conceit of false knowledge, how could there be a direct experience of that oneness of Śiva and the individual soul? (16)

How could that oneness with the essence of bliss through devotion—which is designated as the identity of the individual soul and Brahman—possibly arise for a proponent of non-duality who is devoid of devotion? (17)
Satisfied with mere intellectual knowledge alone and devoid of the practice of meditation, they then prattle about "pure non-duality," saying, "We are of the nature of Brahman. (18)
Therefore, since the proponents of non-duality abide within a single portion of the Veda, one should cast aside envy toward them and take refuge in the non-duality of Śiva. (19)

In the non-dual monistic doctrine of Śiva, through the harmonious convergence of all the Vedas and by direct personal experience alone, one shall attain the bliss of liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
Co said: "O True Guru, the meaning of the word 'yoga' has been understood by me very clearly;
however, [I wish to know] the Patañjala Yoga which is explicitly endowed with its eight limbs. (21)
Meditation is declared to be appropriate for that very purpose when unity arises; how then could one accomplish that state of oneness with Śiva through the practice of meditation? (22)
O Yogin, lover of your devotees, let this be explained in detail;
O my Lord, you alone are able to sever my doubt. (23)
Cidghana said:
"O tiger among kings, that which you have spoken regarding the Pātañjala system can indeed be attained by those seeking liberation through great effort. (24)
Nevertheless, in such a yoga, the term "yoga" is not used in the sense of union;
rather, it would be according to the sequence taught in Sāṃkhya, having the sense of dissociation as it truly stands. (25)
In the state of the perfect equilibrium between Śiva and the individual soul (jīva), which is endowed with the singular bliss of devotion,
the purpose of yoga as described in the practice of meditative concentration (dhyānayoga) is indeed not applicable.

Although meditation is a means within the eightfold yoga, in reality it is not a means for direct perception; rather, such a means is impossible except through the identity of Śiva and the individual soul. || 27 ||
The separation of the Puruṣa and Prakṛti is called Yoga;
how then can meditation on the unity of Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) become a means [to that]? (28)
The knowledge that arises through the continuity of meditation on the identity [of the self] is the means for the state of equilibrium between Śiva and the individual soul,
like the union of a worm and a bee.

Those devoted to the yoga of meditation say that the wearing of the *liṅga* is the gateway to the state called *sāmarasya* (equilibrium) within *samādhi*, and that it is the means for achieving that meditation.
From meditation comes its retention; from that, indeed, concentration which is oneness with Śiva.
Therefore, one should perform internal retention of the Liṅga, the Supreme Self. || 31 ||
Whether capable of internal retention or not, one who observes the vow of Śiva should wear that liṅga for the sake of attaining external goals such as the various *lakṣyas*.
"May I become a bearer of the gods for the sake of immortality"— from this statement,
the wearing of the *liṅga* is declared for the sake of liberation, both externally and internally.
The reality (tattva) proclaimed by Pāṇimanta consists of nine liṅgas and nine kīlakas,
existing as nine cakras through the distinction between the external and the internal.
The wearing of the *liṅga* has been declared as that which awakens the realization of the oneness of the *liṅga* and the body;
therefore, one should wear the supreme *liṅga* according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures. (35)

Oṃ, obeisance to the Lord of Destruction; obeisance to him who is near the Lord of Destruction. Oṃ, obeisance to the Upright One; obeisance to the one whose *liṅga* is upright. Oṃ, obeisance to the Golden One; obeisance to the one whose *liṅga* is golden.
Oṃ, obeisance to the Auspicious-Gold One; obeisance to the one whose *liṅga* is made of auspicious gold. Oṃ, obeisance to the Divine One; obeisance to the one whose *liṅga* is divine.
Salutation! Oṃ, salutation to Bhava, salutation to the Liṅga of Bhava;

Oṃ, salutation to Śarva, salutation to the Liṅga of Śarva; Oṃ, salutation to Śiva, salutation to the Liṅga of Śiva; Oṃ, salutation to Jvala, salutation to the Liṅga of Jvala; Oṃ, salutation to Ātman, salutation to the Liṅga of Ātman. Oṃ.
"Salutation to the Supreme; salutation to the Supreme Liṅga. This purifying Pāṇimantra of Soma and Sūrya installs the Universal Liṅga.
Having performed the rites of the eight enclosures while relying upon the duties of a devoted wife, [she attains the goal].
Through devotion to Śiva and meditation on Śiva, one should take refuge in the yoga of Śiva. || 36 ||
The union of the *liṅga* and the body is the yogi; he is called a practitioner of meditative yoga (*dhyānayogin*).
Therefore, through the power of devotion, one should attain the bliss of the identity of the *liṅga* and the body. (37)
Indeed, the practice of yoga is fruitless when the supreme reality is not known;
and indeed, the practice of yoga is fruitless even when the supreme reality is known. (38)
Therefore, by means of the path of the six stages and through the sequence of meditative yoga,
one attains realization through the experience of the *iṣṭaliṅga*, the *prāṇaliṅga*, and the *bhāvaliṅga*.
Constantly engaged in the practice of reciting the great mantra spoken by the true guru,
the yogi who is ever devoted to Śiva shall become liberated while living.
He said:
"O Lord, the entire sequence of the path of yoga has been well understood by me;
because of the power of your awakening, I have no doubt regarding it. (41)
Therefore, explain everything in such a way that the sequence of meditation and yoga taught in the path of the six stages may be accomplished by me quickly. (42)
Ciddhana said:
This Liṅga, which is identical with the Supreme Brahman, is called the "Station" (Sthala). Its portions, known as individual souls (jīvas), are like sparks from a fire. (43)
By the word "limb" (aṅga), the parts are designated according to the relationship of part and whole;
and for that which is both the self and the body, it is the denotation of the word "limb. (14)
The individual souls (jīvas) are established by the Veda through the systematic arrangement of the relationship between limbs and the possessor of limbs;
therefore, the souls designated as "limbs" are analyzed within the Supreme Reality (paratattva).
Therefore, in the Āgamas, the sacred site (sthala) is declared to be twofold in due order;
it is understood as being both the object of worship and the worshipper, and as the sign (liṅga) and its constituent parts (aṅga). || 46 ||

The object of worship is declared to be the *liṅga*, and the worshipper is traditionally known as its limb; therein, through the various distinctions of the object of worship, the diversity of worshippers is proclaimed. (47)
The solid Liṅga is the Supreme Brahman, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss;
it is declared to be threefold according to the distinctions of its attributes: Bhāva, Prāṇa, and Iṣṭa.
That which is joined with the digit of bliss (ānanda-kalā) is known as the Bhāva-liṅga; that which is conjoined with the digit of consciousness (cit-kalā) there is declared to be the Prāṇa-liṅga.
The external iṣṭaliṅga is said to be accompanied by the six kalās;
thus, by virtue of being distinguished by these kalās, it becomes worthy of worship as the Supreme.
In deep sleep, it is the Liṅga of Being; in the dream state, it has Prāṇa as its Liṅga;
and in the waking state, it is heard in scripture as the Witness, the Liṅga of the Desired.

Thus, the individual soul, known by the name Aṅgasthala, is said to be threefold according to its various states and so forth; it is the enjoyer of the fruit in accordance with its own respective karma. (52)
The inner controller Śiva, the witness, is celebrated by the word *liṅga*;
the individual soul (*jīva*), who is the enjoyer of the fruit therein, is described by the word *aṅga*. (53)
This is also heard in the Śruti through the mantra "dvā suparṇā":
the individual soul (jīva) is called the transmigrator, while the supreme Śiva is the witness and the conscious one. (54)

Having devoutly assumed that linga, which is consciousness itself in the form of the witness, the best of devotees should worship it through the threefold distinctions of spiritual practice (upāsana). || 55 ||

One should worship continuously by means of the contemplation of the *prāṇaliṅga*; this sequence, along with its authoritative basis, is declared in the meditation on the *dahara* (the small space within the heart). 56.
Based on the distinction of three targets, the threefold worship has been described by Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya in his commentary on the Sūtras.
He said:
"O Sadguru, O Great Lord, O expert in the principles of Śiva! That worship which was described by you as bestowing the fruit of liberation while living—" (58)
O glorious one, how is she to be accomplished by me according to the prescriptions of the scriptures?
O you who are expert in all the scriptures, tell me the means for her attainment. (59)
Cidghana said:
"O best of kings, you have asked well while investigating the means;
for in this matter, the Guru is the great means by which one's own desired goal is accomplished. (60)
Since liberation rests in the hands of his devotees by virtue of his extraordinary compassion, the best of devotees should serve the lotus feet of that true guru. 61.
Through the instruction of the Guru, one should receive the great initiation of Vīraśaiva, which is prescribed in the Mahāpāśupata tradition and awakens one to the Great Mantra.
Having worshipped the *liṅga* three times, twice, or once a day as established, one should mutter its mantra, being intent upon meditation upon it. (63)
Accompanied by the *bandha-mudrā* and relying upon the sequence of the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala-krama*),
one should worship the *prāṇaliṅga* through the power of the experience of the *bhāvaliṅga*.

Having heard the true meaning of statements such as "That thou art" from the instruction of the Guru, and through reflecting upon that with devotion out of the compassionate grace of the True Guru, [the disciple attains realization]. 65.
By destroying the three impurities residing in the three limbs, and by contemplating the three lines (*rekhās*), one is freed from the three states (*avasthās*). || 66 ||

Having directly realized the supreme Śiva, who is identical with the Supreme Brahman, accompanied by Ambā, designated as the essence of the rasa of devotion to Śiva, and endowed with Śiva’s power; || 67 ||
Having attained a state of perfect equilibrium with Śiva through the expansion of his own experience of oneness with the essence of the bliss of Brahman, he rejoices.
[Thus ends the third chapter of the *Śivasiddhāntacandrikā*, composed by the venerable Jagadguru Siddhananjeśa Śivācārya, the sovereign of the illustrious Pūvallī Bhāṣya-siṃhāsana.]
He said:
"I am blessed, I have accomplished my purpose; the nectar of your awakening has been drunk by me.
You alone, O Lord, are my refuge for crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra. (1)
Apart from a teacher such as you, there is no other remover of ignorance,
just as there is nothing other than the sun that can dispel darkness.
O king of great gurus, because my lineage has been uplifted by you through the instruction of the Great Mantra, preceded by the initiation of Śiva.
Therefore, O Teacher of the World, since the world has attained discipline through your power,
please explain to me the true meaning of such statements as "That thou art" (Tattvamasi).
Cidghana said:
O great King Satyendra, your intellect is discerning; you have perceived the true meaning of the great sayings, and I shall explain that to you. (5)
There are four great sayings (mahāvākyas) for the realization of the oneness of the Liṅga;
among them, "That thou art" (tattvamasi) is understood through indirect indication.
In the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, having focused upon Soma,
that [truth] was fully and extensively awakened by the teacher through nine repetitions accompanied by illustrative examples.

That secret meaning which is proclaimed as the essential identity (*sāmarasya*) of the *liṅga* and the *aṅga* is precisely what is defined by the great sentences (*mahāvākya*) such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).
By the word "That" (tat), the Linga is denoted—the Supreme Brahman known as Śiva;
and by the word "Thou" (tvam), the body is denoted—the bound one called the individual soul (jīvātman). || 9 ||
In that regard, the state of aesthetic unification (sāmarasya) is described by the word "eighty" itself;
here, the identity of Śiva and the individual soul (jīva) is cited as having the same meaning. || 10 ||
That Liṅga which is characterized by subtle power is indicated by the word "That" (tat-pada);
and that Aṅga which is characterized by gross power is indicated by the word "Thou" (tvam-pada).

Through the abandonment of subtlety and grossness, and by virtue of being endowed with pure potentiality alone, there is a state of equilibrium between the two; that is what is expressed by the word "Asi" (the Sword).

Therefore, [the identity is established] by virtue of the indicated meaning, by virtue of the grammatical coreferentiality of the words, by virtue of the relation between qualifier and qualified, and by virtue of the relation between the indicator and the indicated. || 13 ||
The state of identity between the Linga and the body, as taught by the "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) and other such [Upanishadic] passages, should be understood;
this meaning of the sentence, as proclaimed by the Guru, is in harmony with the Vedas. (14)
First, when duality between those two has been established, non-duality is proclaimed by the wise;
for through the power of meditation, the individual soul (jīva) wards off the state of duality. (15)
One who has ascended to the state of non-duality perceives the power of Śiva directly;
yet, without spiritual practice (upāsanā), the state of duality does not perish.
How indeed can there be a manifestation of non-duality for one who has fallen into duality?
Those who are solely intent on satisfying their own knowledge through mere verbal ostentation [do not attain it]. (17)

Due to the complete abandonment of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of both the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*), those devoid of their own direct experience declare [the state] to be pure non-duality (*śuddhādvaita*). (18)
Just as an insect may attain the state of a bee through union with a bee, so indeed does the individual soul attain the state of Śiva through union with Śiva. || 19 ||
Consciousness is the nature of the Self, consisting of will, knowledge, and action;
since its nature is unobscured, by whom can its state of Śiva-hood be prevented? (20)
And because the literal connection is untenable, and because the intended meaning is untenable, indication (lakṣaṇā) is asserted only where there is a relationship with the sentence-meaning. (21)

And that [indication] is threefold: indeed, *jahatsvārthā* (abandoning its own meaning), likewise *ajahallakṣaṇā* (not abandoning its own characteristic), and the third is called by the wise *jahatyajahatī* (both abandoning and not abandoning). || 22 ||

Having completely abandoned the literal meaning (vācyārtha) because of its connection with another function, the definition of indication (lakṣaṇā) is stated as in the example "the hamlet on the Gaṅgā," where [the word] refers to the bank. 23.

Without abandoning the literal meaning, because it functions through a relation other than that [literal one], the word "red" (śoṇa) in the expression "the red horse runs" (śoṇo dhāvati) is said to convey its own meaning indirectly. (24)
Because it abandons one part and engages with another part,
this [cognition] "This is that Devadatta" is called 'abandoning-and-not-abandoning' (jahatyajahatī).
Thus, in the statement "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), the third [type of] indication is said to be that which, by abandoning subtlety and grossness, is characterized by a single power. (26)
The wise know that the state of essential identity (sāmarasya) is achieved by merging the liṅga and the body.
This systematic exposition is contained within that which is named Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita.

In this statement of the established doctrine, which is situated between duality and non-duality, the reconciliation [of contradictions] regarding both duality and non-duality is rooted in delusion. (28)
Alternatively, another meaning, distinct from the literal sense, is stated;
for the words "I" and so forth convey the meaning of their respective inner controllers (antaryāmin). (29)
And for whom "self" and "body" are the denotations of the word *aṅga*, because the individual soul (*jīvātman*) is indeed the body of the Great Lord of the universe. (30)
Words that denote the body are denoters of its possessor; therefore, they bring about the awakening of the fact that their expressed meaning culminates in the possessor of the body. (31)

In the cognition "I am fat" or "I am thin," the status of being denoted by terms such as "fat" is held to belong respectively to the individual soul (jīva) and its inner controller (antaryāmin), whether directly or through a mediated succession.

Furthermore, because words such as "I" (aham) are employed by those who have taken refuge in Him, there is no contradiction in the existence of Śiva as the inner controller (antaryāmin) possessing power. || 33 ||

Therefore, in reality, Śiva possesses the status of being denoted by the word "thou" (tvaṃpadavācyatva), because of the non-difference between the two [Śiva and the individual soul] as denotable objects through the sentence "That thou art" (tattvamasi). || 34 ||
The unimpeded state of identity between the *liṅga* and the body is declared;
it is described through direct perception by means of the statement "I am Brahman. (35)
Mahādeva, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss, is in the form of the Liṅga;
whereas the individual soul (jīvātman), constrained by the state of worldly existence, is indeed in the form of the body (Aṅga).
By the word "That" (tat), Sadāśiva in the form of the Liṅga is denoted by the wise;
by the word "Thou" (tvam), the individual soul (jīva) characterized by transmigratory existence in the form of the body is indeed meant. (37)
That which is the meaning of "you," whose nature is the limbs [of the body], is indeed the meaning of the word "I.
O Supreme Lord, you who are the indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha) of the words "you" and "I" are the very form of consciousness.

Because the objects denoted by the words "you" (tvam) and "I" (aham)—namely, the physical body and so forth—are contradictory both in terms of their respective words and their actual referents, there can be no realization [of identity]. (39)
The referent indicated by the words "you" and "I" is the individual soul (jīvātman), which is a subordinate form [of the Self];
if it were inauspicious, it would never behold eternal bliss. (40)
Thus, by taking the primary denotative meaning, there indeed exists the identity of "I" and Brahman for the word "I" (aham), as heard directly and through tradition.
Regarding the statement "Brahman is consciousness," that consciousness endowed with the power of wisdom (prajñā-śakti) is the liṅga of existence; it is called the Supreme Brahman. || 42 ||
Regarding the phrase "by which one sees," that sixfold sign consisting of one's own senses and so forth is declared to be the *bhāvaliṅga*. || 43 ||
"This is Brahmā, this is Indra," and so forth—by this [statement], having first established that the entire world-form is grounded therein, he then [proceeds further]. (44)
From the statement "established in wisdom," the power of wisdom (prajñā-śakti) is proclaimed;
therefore, through the distinction of that power, Brahman as consciousness (prajñāna) is made known. || 45 ||
In the passage "This Self is Brahman," the individual soul (jīvātman) is the one named Aṅga,
while the Supreme Brahman in the form of the Liṅga is that which is heard in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad.
Due to its connection with the three bodies and its association with the three states, this individual soul (jīvātman), which is denoted by the limbs [of the mantra], is called "Ātman. || 47 ||
Devoid of a body, manifestly free from the three states, the fourth (turiya), which is indeed denoted by the subtle body (liṅga), is Śiva; he is called Brahman. || 48 ||

Therefore, having always ascertained in truth that the fourth, whose name begins with 'Vā' (Vāmana), is indeed Śiva himself by taking both the indicated meaning and the literal meaning, [one should worship him]. 49.
With the realization "I am Śiva," the devotee who has taken refuge in the state of Śiva attains the bliss of Brahman, the non-duality of Śiva, and the state of Śiva. (50)
He said:
"O illustrious Guru, O great Lord, expert in the Vedas and Agamas!
By the power of your compassion, this awakening through the Great Sayings (mahāvākya) has been understood. (51)
O Ocean of Mercy, tell me how the union of all limbs and the *liṅga* can belong to the individual soul (*jīvātman*), so that through this liberation may become firm. (52)
Cidghana said: O King, listen, O highly fortunate one, crest-jewel of the devotees of Śiva!
Who else on earth besides someone like you would there be to speak of that which is secret? (53)
"All this, whatever exists, is to be pervaded by the Lord"—thus it is declared in the Śruti;
and this limb is heard to consist of the Liṅga denoted by the word "Lord. (54)
Indeed, when that emblem has been abandoned, you must never eat;
do not accept another emblem, lest you live for a hundred years [in bondage].
Even at the cost of sacrificing your life, always become one with the Liṅga;
or else, by wearing this Liṅga and performing a hundred thousand recitations (lakṣajapa), become happy.

One should worship the well-consecrated *sveṣṭaliṅga* as the limb of renunciation (*tyāgāṅga*), the *prāṇaliṅga* as the limb of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*), and the *bhāvaliṅga* as the limb of yoga (*yogāṅga*).
Thus, the Vīraśaiva should always worship the three liṅgas, which are sixfold according to the divisions of his own *kalās*, with devotion in accordance with the prescribed rule. (58)
In the Ādhāra, characterized by right conduct and accompanied by the syllable 'Na' and the Praṇava, the nose—the gateway of the senses—is to be constantly worshipped by devotees. (59)
In the Svādiṣṭhāna [cakra], the Guru-liṅga, radiant with the Praṇava in the form of the syllable *M*,
whose mouth is the organ of the tongue, is to be constantly worshipped by those great lords.
In Maṇipūra, the Śiva-liṅga, which is the locus of the syllable *śikāra* and the *praṇava*, has the eye-faculty as its mouth; it should be worshipped with devotion by those who seek grace. (61)
The unstruck (anāhata) Linga, shining with the Praṇava in the form of 'Vā', having the sense of touch as its mouth, is beautiful and should be worshipped by those who possess the Prāṇalinga. || 62 ||
The Liṅga is Viśuddhi, the Prāsāda mantra accompanied by the syllable 'ya' and the Praṇava;
it is the divine mouth of the faculty of hearing, which should always be worshipped by those seeking refuge.
In the *ājñācakra*, the great *liṅga* resplendent with the syllable *oṃ* and the *praṇava* should always be worshipped with devotion through the unification of the mind and the senses. (64)
Thus, one who is devoted to his own worship, relying upon the three marks (liṅgas),
[attains success] through the performance of worship with devotion and by offering the six essential articles.
Because the three impurities have been burnt away by the three initiations,
one should worship the chosen *liṅga* in the lotus of the hand according to the proper ritual procedure.
Then, devoted to the recitation of mantras and desiring the bliss of liberation, the devotee,
following the sequence taught by the true guru, performed the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa) and other rites.
Having fixed the external focal point upon the chosen Liṅga with a concentrated mind,
one should maintain the internal focal point within the Prāṇa-liṅga, which is adorned by the lotus of the heart.
Having meditated upon the symbol of existence (bhāvaliṅga) according to the internal mark,
one should recite the five-syllabled mantra while contemplating with an unwavering mind.
One should mutter the five-syllabled mantra in secret; one must never utter it aloud.
Otherwise, one will not attain oneness [with the deity] and shall go to the Raurava hell. (70)

Then, by means of stability in meditation, one should perform concentration (dhāraṇā) after holding within the *prāṇaliṅga* a mass of light projected from the form of one's chosen deity (*iṣṭaliṅga*).
Beyond that darkness, appearing like a mass of light,
it manifests itself most wonderfully through its union with the Bhāva-liṅga.
In the *iṣṭaliṅga*, through the external focal point (*bahir-lakṣya*), the *sat-kalā* attains stability;
in the *prāṇaliṅga*, through the internal focal point (*madhya-lakṣya*), the *cit-kalā* becomes manifest and stable. (73)
From the internal object of focus within the linga of being, the digit of the bliss of one's own self flashes forth.
In this sequence, the true devotee, through devotion, attains oneness with the essence of the nectar of bliss.
Having attained the state of the solid liṅga through its form of truth, consciousness, and bliss by means of Śiva-yoga, he shall become liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Every limb consists of the Liṅga, and the entire world consists of the Liṅga;
he perceives the conjunction of the Liṅga in every limb as being in the form of the Liṅga.
In that state, what delusion or grief can there be for one who perceives oneness?
For the yogi of Śiva, the accomplishment of goals both here and in the hereafter arises. || 77 ||
Having abandoned attachment to that [world] and attained the fulfillment of his own desire, which is the abode of Śiva,
he rejoices directly and shall become Śiva himself.
Thus [is] the supreme secret, the realization of the teacher who is a mass of consciousness;
the exceedingly profound and inaccessible reality of the non-duality of Śiva.
Having heard this with unwavering devotion to Śiva and practicing it accordingly,
that king indeed became a possessor of liberation while still alive (jīvanmukta).
[For Cannavīrā Mahādevī and for Cikkaneśvara,] this *Siddhāntacandrikā* has been proclaimed for the sole purpose of attaining the knowledge of Śiva. || 80 ||
[Completed]
